summary: Return the number of words in the shortest chain from beginWord to endWord where each step changes one letter and every intermediate word is in wordList, or 0.
mainInsight: Words are nodes and one-letter changes are unweighted edges, so BFS from beginWord finds the shortest chain. Generate neighbours by trying the 26 letters at each position and checking a word set, instead of comparing against every word.
invariant: When a word at level d is popped, d is the length of the shortest chain from beginWord to it, and every word with a shorter chain has already been enqueued.

approaches.name: Build the graph by comparing all pairs, then BFS
approaches.summary: For every pair of words count differing letters to build edges.
weaknesses: Quadratic in the word count (5000^2 pairs)

approaches.name: BFS with letter substitution
approaches.summary: For each popped word try every letter at every position and keep candidates that are in the word set and unseen.

approaches.name: Bidirectional BFS
approaches.summary: Expand alternately from both ends, always the smaller frontier, and stop when they meet.
approaches.timeComplexity: O(N * L^2 * 26) worst case, far less in practice

approaches.name: Wildcard buckets
approaches.summary: Group words by patterns like h*t; neighbours are the words sharing a bucket.

personalSolution.approach: BFS with letter substitution, trying only letters that appear at that position in wordList
personalSolution.notes: Optimal. Restricting each position to letters seen there is a neat pruning. The dist dict is redundant with a level counter, and checking endWord in the dictionary up front would return 0 early.

commonMistakes: Using DFS, which finds a path but not the shortest one without exploring everything.
Comparing each word with every other word to find neighbours (quadratic).
Returning the number of transformations instead of the number of words (off by one).
Forgetting the early return when endWord is not in wordList.
Marking words visited only when popped, so a word is queued many times.
edgeCases: endWord is one letter away from beginWord -> 2.

promptVariants: Why is DFS a poor choice here even though it can find a valid chain?
What does BFS guarantee that DFS does not?
options: BFS reaches each word first via a shortest chain
DFS cannot handle cycles in the word graph
DFS uses more memory than BFS on this graph
BFS checks fewer neighbours per word than DFS
cards.answer: BFS reaches each word first via a shortest chain
cards.explanation: BFS processes words in order of distance, so the first time endWord is reached is optimal. DFS may find a long chain first and would need to explore all chains to be sure.

incorrectOptionExplanations.DFS cannot handle cycles in the word gra: A visited set handles cycles for either search.
incorrectOptionExplanations.DFS uses more memory than BFS on this gr: BFS usually uses more memory (wide frontiers); memory is not the reason.
incorrectOptionExplanations.BFS checks fewer neighbours per word tha: Both generate the same neighbours per word.

promptVariants: With up to 5000 words of length at most 10, how should you find a word's neighbours?
What is the cheaper way to enumerate words one letter away?
options: Try 26 letters at each position and look the result up in a set
Compare the word with every dictionary word letter by letter
Sort the dictionary and binary search for each neighbour
Precompute edit distance between all pairs of words
cards.answer: Try 26 letters at each position and look the result up in a set
cards.explanation: That is 26 * L <= 260 candidates per word with O(1) set lookups, independent of the 5000-word dictionary size.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Compare the word with every dictionary w: That is N * L per word, so N^2 * L overall: 25 million pairs.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Sort the dictionary and binary search fo: You still need to generate candidates; a hash set already gives O(1) lookups.
incorrectOptionExplanations.Precompute edit distance between all pai: Quadratic in N and edit distance is more than needed (only substitutions).

promptVariants: beginWord = "a", endWord = "c", wordList = ["a", "b", "c"]. What is returned?
What is the answer for "a" -> "c" with wordList ["a", "b", "c"]?
cards.explanation: "a" -> "c" is a single letter change and "c" is in the list, so the chain has two words.

incorrectOptionExplanations.1: The count includes beginWord, so even one step gives 2.
incorrectOptionExplanations.3: That would go through "b", which is not shortest.
incorrectOptionExplanations.0: endWord is in the list and reachable.

promptVariants: If endWord is ___ wordList, return 0 immediately before any BFS.

cards.explanation: Every word of the chain after beginWord, including endWord, must be in wordList.

promptVariants: How does bidirectional BFS speed this up, and when do you stop?
Explain bidirectional BFS for Word Ladder.
cards.answer: Keep two frontiers, one from beginWord and one from endWord. Each round expand the smaller frontier by one level; when a generated word is in the other frontier, the chain length is the sum of both depths + 1. Searching from both sides explores about 2 * b^(d/2) words instead of b^d.
cards.explanation: It needs endWord known up front, which this problem gives.

promptVariants: N words of length L. What is the running time of the canonical code?
Derive the time complexity of BFS with letter substitution.
cards.explanation: Each of up to N words is popped once; it builds 26 * L candidates and each slice-and-concatenate plus hash costs O(L).

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(N^2 * L): That is the pairwise-comparison graph build.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(N * L * 26): Misses that building and hashing each candidate string costs O(L).
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(26^L): That is the number of all possible strings; BFS only visits dictionary words.

cards.explanation: Each container holds at most N strings of length L.
